result:
Lately I've been thinking about unfinished things.

Not in a sad way. In a fond way. The half-read book with a train ticket still tucked in it as a bookmark. The sketchbook where the first ten pages are full and frantic and beautiful, and the rest is just blank paper waiting very patiently. The language app abandoned at lesson fourteen of Portuguese — just enough to say *bom dia* and *onde fica a praia?* and feel, for a second, like a slightly different version of yourself might exist.

We tend to treat unfinished things as failures with good PR. Projects we didn't stick to. Habits we didn't build. But I wonder if some of them were never supposed to be finished. Maybe they were just supposed to be *started*, long enough for us to brush up against an idea and carry a little of it away.

I knew a man once — well, I heard about a man, which is almost the same thing — who spent eleven years building a sailboat in his backyard in Ohio. Not near a lake big enough to matter. Just in his backyard, between the fence and the apple tree. Neighbors asked when he was going to launch it. He always said, "Next summer, maybe." He caulked it, sanded it, painted its name on the stern in careful blue letters: *Wanderer*. 

He never launched it. And I don't think that makes the story sadder. I think he *was* sailing it, the whole time. Every evening after work, he got to stand inside a future and hammer nails into it. The boat didn't need water. It needed a place to go in his head that wasn't work, or bills, or getting older.

We all have a version of that boat.

A garden that is mostly plans and three heroic tomato plants. A novel in a document called "FINAL_v7_REAL.docx" that is really just three perfect opening paragraphs you reread when you want to remember that you can make things. A friendship that faded not with a fight but with life getting loud, and yet you still think of them instantly when you hear a certain song, so in some way that conversation never actually ended.

I like the way unfinished things stay open. A finished thing has to be judged. It has to be good or bad, successful or a flop. An unfinished thing still gets to be pure possibility. It hasn't disappointed anyone yet. Inside it, you are still brilliant and committed and young and full of time.

There is also something honest about them. Life is not, for most of us, a series of clean completions. It's mostly middles. We are in the middle of raising kids, in the middle of grieving people, in the middle of learning how to be the person we swore we'd be by thirty-five, now quietly renegotiating the deadline. The finished projects are the exceptions we put on shelves. The unfinished ones are the furniture we actually live among.

So I'm learning to be less embarrassed by mine. The scarf that is twelve inches long and will never know a neck. The list of recipes clipped for a dinner party that exists only theoretically, where everyone I love is free on the same night and nobody is allergic to anything. The running shoes that have done more walking to coffee shops than running anywhere, but have still, technically, taken me outside more than I would have gone without them.

None of those things failed me. They just worked at a smaller scale than I advertised.

If anything, I wish we kept them more tenderly. Not hidden in a closet of shame, but out where we can see them: proof that at various points in our lives we were curious enough to begin. That we saw something — a language, a boat, a better morning routine, a braver version of a story — and thought, *maybe me too*.

Maybe me too is enough, sometimes.

The rest can stay beautifully, unapologetically unfinished.
